Two questions, not one

Christians who agree on the creeds still disagree about the "last things". Most of the disagreement comes down to two separate questions. When is the thousand years of Revelation 20? And how should we read the book of Revelation?
The inner ring: the millennium

Four answers place Christ’s return relative to the "thousand years". He returns after it (postmillennial). The millennium is the present age (amillennial). Or he returns before it (premillennial, in historic and dispensational forms).
Christ reigns now. Through the gospel and the Spirit, the nations will be largely discipled before he returns at the end of a long era of blessing.
The thousand years is symbolic of the whole church age. Satan is bound so the gospel goes to the nations, and the saints reign with Christ. One return brings resurrection, judgment and new creation.

Christ returns before a future earthly kingdom. Historic premillennialists usually see one return after the tribulation. Dispensationalists distinguish Israel and the church, and most expect a rapture before the tribulation.
The outer ring: reading Revelation

Preterists see much of the book as fulfilled in the first century. Historicists see it unfolding across church history, futurists mostly at the end, and idealists in timeless patterns. Eclectic readers blend these approaches.
The threads: how they combine
The axes combine. Gold threads mark common pairings, such as partial preterist with postmillennial, futurist with dispensational, and idealist with amillennial. Dashed threads are rare.

The prologue and the vision of the risen Son of Man
Prologue and inaugural vision

Revelation opens by naming itself a revelation of Jesus Christ given through an angel to John, with a blessing on those who read it aloud and keep it, because the time is near. A letter greeting from the eternal God, the sevenfold Spirit and Jesus Christ leads into a doxology and a prophetic announcement that Christ is coming with the clouds. John, exiled on Patmos, is caught up 'in the Spirit' on the Lord's day and sees the glorified Son of Man walking among seven golden lampstands, a figure combining Daniel's Son of Man and Ancient of Days. Christ commissions him to write what he sees to the seven churches and explains the stars and lampstands.
Title, chain of revelation and first beatitude
Letter greeting, doxology and the coming of Christ
John on Patmos, in the Spirit on the Lord's day
Vision of one like a Son of Man among the lampstands
Fear, reassurance and commission; the mystery of stars and lampstands

Chapter 1 sets the frame for the whole book. Its opening words echo Daniel 2:28-29, where God reveals to Nebuchadnezzar 'what must happen in the latter days'; John's version, 'what must soon come to pass', is read by many as a deliberate claim that Daniel's latter days have begun. The chain of revelation (God, Christ, angel, John, servants) mirrors Jewish apocalypses, which use angelic mediators, but John writes in his own name, as a prophet, to real congregations. The greeting turns the divine name of Exodus 3:14 into a threefold title, the doxology applies Israel's calling as a kingdom of priests (Exodus 19:6) to those freed by Jesus' blood, and Revelation 1:7 fuses Daniel 7:13 with Zechariah 12:10. The inaugural vision is built from Daniel 7 and 10, Ezekiel 1 and 43, and Zechariah 4: Christ wears the priest's long robe and walks among the lampstands as a priest tending the temple lights, while bearing attributes that in Daniel belong to God himself.

The Greco-Roman backdrop is equally present. Patmos was a small island off Miletus with a Roman garrison, and banishment to an island (relegatio) was a common Roman penalty. Ephesus, Smyrna and Pergamum all competed for imperial temples, and emperors were hailed with titles of saviour, lord and son of god; Revelation's claims that Jesus is 'ruler of the kings of the earth' and holds the keys of Death and Hades confront that ideology. The seven stars in the right hand may evoke imperial coins on which a deified emperor's child or the emperor is shown with stars, and Hecate, a goddess honoured in Asia, was said to hold the keys of Hades. Each element of the vision is reused in the opening titles of the seven letters that follow.
The revelation of Jesus Christ

Greek apokalypsis translates the idea of God 'uncovering' secrets, as in Daniel 2:19-30 (Theodotion uses apokalyptō), where God 'reveals mysteries' about the latter days. Jewish apocalypses (1 Enoch, 4 Ezra, 2 Baruch) share this disclosure through visions and angels.
In ordinary Greek the word meant unveiling or disclosure; it was not yet a technical name for a literary genre, a sense that later grew from this very book.

The book is an unveiling that comes from Jesus Christ (given him by God) and also concerns him. Grammatically 'of Jesus Christ' can be subjective (Christ reveals) or objective (Christ revealed); most commentators think both are intended. It frames all that follows as divine disclosure, not human speculation.
What must soon come to pass ... the time is near

Daniel 2:28 (Septuagint) speaks of what must happen 'in the last days'; John substitutes 'soon'. Daniel 12:4 told Daniel to seal up the book until the time of the end, whereas John is told the time is near (Revelation 22:10). Prophets often announced the nearness of the day of the LORD (Joel 1:15; Zephaniah 1:14).

John says the events revealed are imminent and pressing for the first hearers. How 'soon' and 'near' relate to events still unfulfilled is one of the most contested questions in the book, and the answer largely determines one's interpretive school.

The time words should be taken at face value: the bulk of the prophecy, especially the judgment on Jerusalem and the persecuting powers, was fulfilled within the first hearers' lifetime (AD 66–70, with Rome also in view). The same words bracket the book (Revelation 22:6, 10), so they govern its main content, though the final consummation in chapters 20–22 lies beyond.
'Soon' governs the entire book, including the Second Coming and new creation, so all of it was fulfilled by AD 70; proponents argue that any delay empties the time statements of meaning.

'Soon' can mean 'quickly' (suddenly once it begins) or reflect God's perspective in which a thousand years are as a day (2 Peter 3:8); the nearness is the imminence of the last days, which began with Christ and may culminate at any time.
The time is always near because the conflict John describes is constantly present; each generation lives at the threshold of the end, and the call to readiness applies to all.
The latter days foretold in Daniel were inaugurated by Christ's death and resurrection (already), so the fulfilment has begun 'soon', while its consummation is still awaited (not yet).
Blessed is the one who reads aloud
Public reading of Scripture was central to synagogue worship (Nehemiah 8:1-8; Luke 4:16-21; Acts 15:21). Beatitudes ('blessed is the one who...') are a wisdom form common in the Psalms (Psalm 1:1).
Most people in the first century could not read; letters were read aloud to gathered households and assemblies (Colossians 4:16).

This is the first of seven beatitudes in Revelation (1:3; 14:13; 16:15; 19:9; 20:6; 22:7; 22:14). It assumes the book will be read aloud in worship and pronounces blessing not on understanding alone but on hearing and keeping it, showing the book's practical, pastoral aim.
The seven churches in the province of Asia
Seven signals completeness from the creation week (Genesis 1–2:3). Old Testament prophets addressed nations and cities in series (Amos 1–2).
Asia was the wealthy Roman province on the Aegean coast of modern Turkey, with Ephesus as its leading city. The seven cities lie on a circular road in the order a courier would follow from Ephesus.

Seven literal congregations are addressed, but the number and the refrain 'to the churches' indicate that they also represent the whole church. The book was meant for all seven, and through them for others.
Some historicists and many older dispensationalists see the seven churches also as prophetic of seven successive eras of church history, from apostolic Ephesus to lukewarm modern Laodicea.
The seven stand for the universal church in every age, displaying the recurring strengths and failures of Christian communities.
Him who is and was and is to come

An expansion of the divine name in Exodus 3:14 ('I AM WHO I AM'; Septuagint: 'I am the one who is'). Palestinian Targums on Exodus 3:14 and Deuteronomy 32:39 contain similar threefold paraphrases (the Targums are later, though they may preserve older traditions).
Greeks applied 'was, is and will be' to Zeus (Pausanias 10.12.10) and to deities in inscriptions; John's version is distinctive because the third member is not 'will be' but 'is coming'.

God is eternal and sovereign over past, present and future, but the future is expressed as his coming to set things right. John deliberately keeps the divine name grammatically unchanged after the preposition, a 'solecism' most scholars think is intentional reverence for the name.
The seven Spirits before His throne

Zechariah 4:2-10 has a lampstand with seven lamps that are 'the eyes of the LORD ranging through all the earth' and the word 'not by might nor by power but by my Spirit'. Isaiah 11:2 (Septuagint) lists sevenfold gifts of the Spirit resting on the Messiah. Jewish texts also knew seven chief angels (Tobit 12:15; 1 Enoch 20).

Placed between the Father and Jesus Christ in a Trinitarian-shaped greeting, the seven Spirits most likely represent the Holy Spirit in his fullness and active presence in all the churches (Revelation 4:5; 5:6). A minority view identifies them as seven archangels.
The faithful witness, the firstborn from the dead, and the ruler of the kings of the earth

Psalm 89:27 and 89:37 promise David's heir will be God's 'firstborn, the highest of the kings of the earth' and established like 'the faithful witness in the sky'. The three titles summarise Jesus' death (witness), resurrection (firstborn) and enthronement (ruler).

Roman emperors claimed rule over client kings; John claims that the crucified and risen Jesus, not Caesar, rules the kings of the earth. 'Witness' (martys) later came to mean martyr, partly through this book.

Jesus is the model of faithful testimony even to death, the first to rise in resurrection life, and the present king above all earthly kings. The titles set the pattern for the churches: to bear witness as he did and to share his victory.

Christ already reigns as ruler of the kings of the earth since his ascension; partial preterists who are also postmillennial (Gentry, Mathison) see this present kingship as undergirding an expectation of the gospel's growing triumph in history, while amillennial partial preterists stress the same reign without that expectation.
Christ holds the title by right now, but its full public exercise over the nations awaits his return and earthly kingdom (Revelation 19–20).
The title assures persecuted believers in every age that the powers which oppress them are already subject to the risen Christ.
A kingdom, priests to His God and Father

Exodus 19:6 calls Israel, freed from Egypt, a 'kingdom of priests and a holy nation'. Isaiah 61:6 promises restored Israel will be called 'priests of the LORD'. The language also recalls the Passover deliverance by the blood of the lamb.

By his blood Jesus has freed people and made them, now, a royal priesthood, taking up the vocation of Exodus 19:6 (how this relates to national Israel's own calling is read differently by covenantal and dispensational interpreters). This is a present status (the verb is past tense), anticipating its fuller form in Revelation 5:10 and 20:6.
Believers already reign and serve as priests with Christ; the 'reign' of Revelation 20 describes this present heavenly and spiritual kingship.
The church shares this priestly status, but it should not be merged with national Israel's distinct promises, which await a future literal kingdom.
The present kingship of the saints expresses itself in history as the gospel advances and Christ's rule extends through his people.
He is coming with the clouds ... even those who pierced Him

Combines Daniel 7:13 (one like a son of man coming with the clouds of heaven to the Ancient of Days) and Zechariah 12:10-14 (the house of David and Jerusalem look on the one they pierced and mourn, tribe by tribe, 'the land' mourning). In the Old Testament, God 'rides on the clouds' in judgment (Isaiah 19:1; Psalm 104:3). Jesus combined the same texts in Matthew 24:30.

A prophetic announcement of Christ's coming in power and judgment, seen by those responsible for his death. John widens Zechariah's mourning to 'all the tribes of the earth'. The Greek word ge can mean 'earth' or 'land' (of Israel), and whether the mourning is repentance or remorse is debated. Which coming is meant is a central dispute.

Primarily a coming in judgment on first-century Jerusalem (AD 70), on the generation that pierced him; 'tribes of the land' means the tribes of Israel, and 'clouds' is Old Testament language for divine judgment (Isaiah 19:1). Many add that it also foreshadows the final bodily return.
This is the one Second Coming, fulfilled in AD 70 in the destruction of Jerusalem; there is no further visible return.
The visible, personal Second Coming at the end of the tribulation, when every eye will literally see him; Zechariah 12 points to a future national repentance of Israel.
The final personal advent at the close of the prophetic history, the goal toward which all the seals, trumpets and vials move.
The final, worldwide return of Christ (Revelation 19), while Daniel 7:13 also speaks of his enthronement already begun; the 'mourning' may include both repentance and judgment.
I am the Alpha and the Omega ... the Almighty

Isaiah 41:4, 44:6 and 48:12: 'I am the first and I am the last.' Later rabbinic tradition said the Hebrew word for truth (emet) spans the first, middle and last letters of the alphabet, to show God is from beginning to end (Genesis Rabbah 81, later material). 'Almighty' (pantokratōr) is the Septuagint's rendering of 'LORD of hosts' and 'Shaddai'.
Pantokratōr ('ruler of all') echoed and outbid claims of imperial power; the letters A and Ω had a use in Greek mystical texts as signs of totality.

God is the source and goal of all history, sovereign over everything. Later in the book Jesus uses the same title (Revelation 22:13), placing him on the divine side of the line between Creator and creation, a key datum for New Testament Christology.
On the island of Patmos
Prophets often received visions in exile or by rivers away from the land (Ezekiel 1:1 by the Chebar; Daniel 10:4 by the Tigris).

Patmos was a small rocky island about 60 km from Miletus, with a garrison, a temple of Artemis and a settled population; it was not a deserted penal colony. Roman governors could sentence people to relegation on islands. Victorinus (c. 260) says John was sentenced to labour in mines there under Domitian; the tradition is late but early in Christian memory.

John is on Patmos 'because of the word of God and the testimony of Jesus', most naturally meaning exiled for his preaching, though some suggest he went there to preach. As a 'partner in the tribulation and kingdom and perseverance', he shares the churches' situation.
Banishment fits Nero's reign (c. 64–68) and a church entering 'the tribulation' of the 60s; later traditions placing the exile under Nero are cited in support.
Most futurists accept the Domitianic tradition (c. 95); John's tribulation is the general suffering of believers, distinct from the future Great Tribulation.
Partner in the tribulation and kingdom and perseverance
Daniel 7:21-27 pictures the saints suffering under a hostile power yet receiving the kingdom. Jewish expectation linked the 'messianic woes' of distress with the arrival of the kingdom.

One Greek article governs all three nouns, binding them together: believers share in Christ's kingdom now, in the midst of tribulation, and the way of the kingdom is patient endurance. This combination shapes the book's ethic.
'The tribulation' is the specific great tribulation coming on that generation (Matthew 24:21), which John and his readers are entering.
John speaks of the ordinary tribulation of believers in this age, which is distinct from the future seven-year Tribulation described from chapter 6.
Tribulation and kingdom are simultaneous throughout the church age: the saints reign while they suffer, which is the pattern of Revelation 20.
On the Lord's day
The prophets spoke of 'the day of the LORD', the coming day of judgment and salvation (Joel 2:31; Amos 5:18). The Sabbath was Israel's holy day.

In Asia Minor some cities marked a monthly or annual 'Augustus' day' (Sebastē) in honour of the emperor; a Christian 'Lord's day' implicitly contrasts with it. Early Christian writers use 'Lord's day' (kyriakē hēmera) for Sunday, the resurrection day (Didache 14.1; Ignatius, Magnesians 9.1).

Most interpreters take it as Sunday, the day of Christian worship; John receives his vision while the churches gather. A minority (including some futurists such as Seiss and E. W. Bullinger) understand it as 'the day of the Lord', meaning John is transported in vision into the eschatological day of judgment, but the Greek adjective differs from the Old Testament phrase.
I was in the Spirit ... a loud voice like a trumpet

Ezekiel is repeatedly lifted by the Spirit into visions (Ezekiel 2:2; 3:12-14; 11:1). A trumpet blast accompanied God's descent at Sinai (Exodus 19:16-19) and announces the day of the LORD (Joel 2:1; Zephaniah 1:16).

John describes a prophetic visionary state under the Spirit's control. The phrase recurs at Revelation 4:2, 17:3 and 21:10, marking major sections. The trumpet-like voice signals a Sinai-like theophany: the voice is Christ's.
Seven golden lampstands

The tabernacle menorah was a single golden lampstand with seven lamps, tended daily by priests (Exodus 25:31-40; Leviticus 24:1-4). Zechariah 4 sees a golden lampstand with seven lamps fed by two olive trees, symbolising Israel's witness empowered by the Spirit. Solomon's temple had ten lampstands (1 Kings 7:49).
Lamps and lampstands were common in homes and temples; the Arch of Titus in Rome (after 81) famously shows the temple menorah carried in triumph after 70.

Christ himself interprets them as the seven churches (Revelation 1:20). The church is God's true temple, a light-bearer whose task is witness, and its light depends on Christ's presence and the Spirit. A lampstand can be removed (Revelation 2:5) if a church ceases to witness.
With the earthly temple's lampstand about to be removed in AD 70, Christ shows that his churches are now the true lampstands of God's house.

The lampstands represent the local churches of the present age; in the dispensational reading the events of chapters 4–22 follow the church's departure at the rapture, while historic premillennial futurists see the church still on earth through them.
One like the Son of Man

From Daniel 7:13, the human-like figure who comes to the Ancient of Days and receives everlasting dominion, and Daniel 10:5-6, the radiant heavenly being by the Tigris. In 1 Enoch 37–71 (the Similitudes) a pre-existent 'Son of Man' sits on the throne of glory and judges; 4 Ezra 13 has a man rising from the sea and flying with the clouds.
Jesus' favourite self-designation in the Gospels. The risen Christ is the Danielic Son of Man who has received the kingdom and now stands among his churches as Lord and judge.
A long robe, with a golden sash around His chest

The high priest's robe reached to the feet (podērēs in the Septuagint of Exodus 28:4, 31 and Zechariah 3:4) and he wore a woven sash. Josephus (Antiquities 3.7.2) describes the priestly girdle wound high on the chest. Daniel 10:5 has a man clothed in linen with a belt of gold.
Long robes also signified dignity for kings and magistrates.

Christ appears as high priest (tending the lampstands) and as king. Some note the sash worn high at the chest rather than the waist signals rest from labour or majestic dignity, but the main point is priestly-royal glory.
Hair white like wool, as white as snow

In Daniel 7:9 the hair of the Ancient of Days is like pure wool and his garment white as snow. 1 Enoch 46:1 and 71:10 describe the 'Head of Days' with hair white as wool. Isaiah 1:18 uses snow and wool for cleansing.
In the ancient world white hair signified age, honour and wisdom.

John applies to the Son of Man an attribute of the Ancient of Days himself, identifying Christ with God's eternity, wisdom and purity. This fusion of Daniel's two figures is one of the boldest Christological moves in the New Testament.
His eyes were like a blazing fire
Daniel 10:6: the heavenly man's eyes are like flaming torches. Fire is associated with God's holiness and judgment (Deuteronomy 4:24).
Christ's piercing sight sees all and judges truly. The image returns for Thyatira (Revelation 2:18, 2:23: he searches minds and hearts) and for the rider on the white horse (Revelation 19:12).
Feet like polished bronze refined in a furnace

Daniel 10:6 (arms and legs like burnished bronze) and Ezekiel 1:7 (the living creatures' feet gleaming like burnished bronze). The 'furnace' may echo Daniel 3, where a divine figure walks in the fiery furnace.

The rare Greek word chalkolibanon is otherwise unknown; Hemer argues it denotes a fine alloy produced by Thyatira's bronze-working guild, which explains why the image heads the Thyatira letter (Revelation 2:18).
Strength, stability, purity and the power to trample enemies; Christ stands firm and treads down evil.
His voice was like the roar of many waters
Ezekiel 43:2: the glory of the God of Israel came, and his voice was like the sound of many waters; compare Ezekiel 1:24 and Daniel 10:6 (voice like the sound of a multitude).

Christ's voice carries the overwhelming majesty of God's own voice. In Ezekiel 43 this voice accompanies God's glory returning to the temple, suggesting Christ's presence among the churches is the glory's return to God's house.
In His right hand seven stars
Stars stand for angels and heavenly beings (Job 38:7; Daniel 8:10; 12:3; 1 Enoch 86). The right hand is the place of power and protection (Psalm 110:1; Isaiah 41:10).

The seven planets (sun, moon and five visible planets) symbolised cosmic rule. A Roman coin of Domitian shows his deceased infant son as a divine child seated on a globe surrounded by seven stars, an image of imperial world-dominion (the coin is post-82, so its relevance depends on dating). Mithraic and astrological imagery also linked seven stars with sovereignty.

Christ, not the emperor or the stars of fate, holds cosmic sovereignty and holds the churches' 'angels' securely in his hand. The stars are interpreted as the angels of the churches (see 'angels of the seven churches').
A sharp double-edged sword came from His mouth

Isaiah 49:2: the Servant's mouth is made 'like a sharp sword'; Isaiah 11:4: the Messiah strikes the earth with the rod of his mouth and slays the wicked with the breath of his lips. Wisdom of Solomon 18:15-16 pictures God's word as a stern warrior with a sharp sword. 4 Ezra 13:10 has the messianic man destroy enemies with a stream of fire from his mouth.

The sword (Latin ius gladii, 'right of the sword') symbolised a Roman governor's power of capital punishment, held by the proconsul of Asia, who held assizes in Pergamum among other cities. The Greek rhomphaia was a long Thracian sword.

Christ's judging and conquering word. His power is exercised by speech, not by military force, and it cuts both ways: it defends his people and judges unfaithful members of his church (Revelation 2:12, 2:16) as well as his enemies (Revelation 19:15, 19:21).
The sword from the mouth signals that Christ conquers the nations through the preached word, a picture of the gospel's progressive triumph in history.
